reviewer: Claude agent review (Fable 5.1), not a human historian
text: 2026-10-11: approved on a fresh full read after the owner's rewrite of the scene prose into pure storytelling (README step 4 rule, 2026-10-11). This review covers text only: the twelve scenes' paragraphs and dramatised lists, the introduction and the summary were rewritten; facts.json and the thirteen pictures are unchanged, so imageSha256 is carried over from the 2026-10-10 approval and the illustrations list below still stands.

The storytelling rule checked: inside a scene events happen in order and with confidence; no 'the poet says', 'the stone does not say', 'historians think', 'disputed' or 'perhaps', and no scholar name in scene prose except in scene-12 (1800 to 1889), where Buchanan, Wellesley, Scanlon and Rice are characters in the events told. Where the record is silent the story chooses one plausible telling and discloses the choice in that scene's dramatised list, which the evidence page prints. A scan of every paragraph, the introduction and the summary for ಕಲ್ಲು ಹೇಳುವುದಿಲ್ಲ, ಇತಿಹಾಸಕಾರ, ವಿವಾದ, ಬಹುಶಃ, ಊಹೆ, ಪ್ರಕಾರ and the names Rice, Narasimhachar, Hultzsch found nothing in prose; the words occur only in dramatised lists and facts, where they belong.

Choices the story makes and where each is disclosed: Nagavarma killed by the Ganga warrior Mudurachayya and avenged (the 1923 reading; Rice's fratricide reading named as the alternative) in scene-01 and scene-03; Chaladankaganga = Mudurachayya (1923) in scene-03; Chavundaraya seating Rachamalla as modern historians' inference with the stone saying only that the design was rendered vain, in scene-03; Chavundaraya standing at the basadi door through Marasimha's three-day fast, with the shared guru Ajitasena as the only basis, in scene-02; the colossus year 981 (Jain tradition) against Rice's 983 from the Purana's silence, in scene-04 and scene-06; the three signature scripts cut on one day although the Nagari line may be of Gangaraja's time (Hultzsch, c. 1116), in scene-07 and scene-11; the Tyagada relief told as Chavundaraya and Nemichandra while the identification is tradition, in scene-08; 'people of his time called it only Gommata' as an inference from the silence of tenth-century stones, in scene-08; Rice's inference that he died before the basadi was finished and that the son finished it as a memorial, against the 1923 edition which also credits the basadi to him, in scene-10; his death by sallekhana as the storyteller's guess, signalled by ಹೋಗಿರಬೇಕು in the text, in scene-10; the two bard scenes as 16th to 19th century legend, a composite of the Bhujabali Charite and the Rajavali Kathe, with the golden arrow and the name Gullakayajji marked modern, in scene-05 and scene-09; the 1231 Yakshi of Bammisetti and the 18th-century tank kept out of the prose and stated in scene-09's note. Invented texture (the night camp and the bone cup, the burning fort being Uchchangi, ten years of war, the throne hall, the writing desk with Nemichandra in the room, the scaffolds and the masons' numbers, the minister watching all day, the sculptor walking down the hill, the Tamil and Nagari lines 'for pilgrims', the enclosure being built, Buchanan's work described, the Waterloo link, all dialogue) is named in each scene's dramatised list.

Every event, name, place, number and year was compared with facts.json and with the verbatim texts in research/ganga-verified.md: no. 109 (Brahma-Kshatra, Vajvala's army fleeing like deer by order of Indra before Jagadekavira, the black serpent my arrow, Chaladanka-Ganga's design, the jewelled skull-cups); no. 38 and the 1923 translation (the Pallava skulls and the Kapalika, Manyakheta, Gonur, Uchchangi, Banavasi, Chera Chola Pandya Pallava, one year more, Ajitasena-bhattaraka of Bankapura, the three-day vow, the Chola and Pandya verse); the Purana colophon titles in both editions and Rice's 'no mention of a single work of religious merit'; Rice's description of the image and the scale 'almost exactly 3 ft 3 1/2 in, or the French metre, evidently the one employed in the original design'; nos. 75-76 in Hultzsch's readings with the sides as Rice gives them; no. 67 with Jinadevana from the 1923 Introduction; no. 89; 'a hundred-fold more fortunate than the former Raya of the Gangas'; 1923 no. 133 on Indra IV (grandson of Krishna III, Marasimha's sister's son, 982, Chandragiri); Buchanan July 1800 (120 houses, the inflammation the day before, the painter and interpreter, 'for the accuracy of which I cannot answer', 70 ft 3 in, Wellesley 'lately', the rock cut till only the image remained, Chamunda Raya ancestor of nine Belalla rajas); Scanlon June 1871 (50 ft, 9 ft, 26 ft, the priests interfered) and Rice's 57 ft; 144 inscriptions; Jaini 1927 on Gommatasara and 'Gommateshvara, the Lord of Gommata'; Rajaraja's Gangapadi and Rajarajapura.

Blockers found on this pass and fixed before approval: scene-10 said Chavundaraya's gurus had also died by sallekhana, which no source read records (only Marasimha, Indra IV and Pullabba are recorded); both sentences now name only his king and his sister. The scene-10 dramatised note had a non-word (ತೆಲ್ಲಿಕೆ), now ಊಹೆ. Nits fixed on the same pass: 'northern wars' dropped from scene-01 (the Khedaga war has no recorded place); the Indra IV sentence in scene-02 now counts nine years from the coronation; Mudurachayya is ಗಂಗರ ವೀರ (Gangara-bhata), not of the Ganga lineage; the 981 note in scene-04 reworded; scene-08 now ends at ಏಕೈಕ ಮುಖ, with the weathering and the invented face moved to its dramatised note.

Kannada: told-story register for adults, no vulgarity; no em dash anywhere; NFC; the skull-cups, the sallekhana deaths, the nude monks and the nude image are covered by the content note, which is truthful. The introduction tells the reader that faces, speech, nights and dust are the storyteller's, that two scenes are legend told by a village bard, and that the last pages separate stone, legend and invention. The summary states only what the scenes chose (Chaladankaganga killed, 981, Jinadevana c. 995, Gangaraja c. 1116) and nothing the scenes do not.

story.facts is byte-identical to facts.json (33 facts); every scene facts[] id and didYouKnow id resolves and every fact is used; each scene's facts[] covers that scene's recorded claims; the disputed notes in facts.json still carry both readings for every contested point, so the evidence page tells the truth about each choice the prose makes.
illustrations: All thirteen WebPs (cover, scene-01 to scene-12, 1600x900) were opened and compared with their scene paragraphs, alt texts and bible/style.md, with enlarged crops of hands, forts, horses, palm leaf, both rock faces, far hills, scaffolds and the village. The owner rejected the first heavy-built design of Chavundaraya; he was redesigned as a tall, strong general with a square jaw, thick moustache, no beard, hair in a knot, grey at the temples and a scar on the left forearm, and seven pictures were replaced (cover, scene-01, scene-03, scene-04, scene-06, scene-07, scene-08); bible/style.md was updated to the new look and the word ದಪ್ಪ removed from the text. The seven replacements were reopened and re-checked; this approval hashes the replaced files.
No image blockers in either set. The first set's only period fault, scene-01's fort as an ashlar castle with square towers, went away with the replacement, which shows rubble walls on a crag.

cover: the general in his fifties at the lotus pedestal, white fillet with upright plume, moustache, scar, straight sword, white dhoti with red border; the colossus's feet, creeper and cobras rising out of frame; a monk seated in a rock shadow in side view with a pichchi; Chandragiri with small shrines and the village across the valley. Nit: the far shrines have small tiered towers and no anthills show round the legs.

scene-01: night camp below a burning rubble hill fort; the general with sword and dagger, the jewelled cup on the rock; elephants in plain cloth, a horse with a cloth saddle and no stirrup, round shields, spears, tents. Clean.
scene-02: thin bearded king in white with the crown on the floor, a monk on a stone bench in side view with a pichchi, guards at a distance, a pillar being raised outside by a timber derrick. Clean.

scene-03: timber court by the river; the young crowned king in pearls; the general with one hand on the throne and one on a straight sword; the Ganga elephant on a red cloth banner; chowrie women; bowing chiefs; a guard in a gold-banded head-wrap. Clean.

scene-04: lamp-lit night, the general greying at the temples incising a palm leaf with a stylus, sword on a cloth, a monk seated in back view in shadow, a moonlit hill in the window. Nit: the leaf carries AI pseudo-strokes, not readable script.

scene-05: white-bearded bard with a drum on Chandragiri's steps, pilgrims, the small colossus silhouette on Vindhyagiri at sunset, village of tiled and thatched houses. Clean for a sixteenth-century frame.

scene-06: head and shoulders of the colossus emerging among rope-lashed timber scaffolds, ringlet hair, long ears, half-open eyes, faint smile, creeper on the arm; masons tiny against it; the minister and a nude monk seen from behind. Nit: small towered shrines on Chandragiri in a tenth-century frame.

scene-07: feet and lotus pedestal; a mason with mallet and chisel over a chalk guide-line and chips, no letters; the minister with folded arms. Nit: the line is cut on the rock below the pedestal rather than on the anthill rock below the hands.

scene-08: the Tyagada pillar base relief of a plumed seated man and a seated monk being carved; the minister on a stone bench, the monk with palm leaves in side view, two chowrie women; the colossus's feet behind. Clean.

scene-09: night, the bard with drum by a lamp, an old woman with a gourd, a natural moonlit pond between the hills, Chandragiri shrines, a village of oil lamps. Clean; the pond is not the eighteenth-century stepped tank.

scene-10: a plain granite basadi being topped out with a pulley derrick, a young man in white at the door, a monk in the doorway shadow, small tiered basadis and a manastambha with a pavilion top, Vindhyagiri with the colossus far off. Clean.

scene-11: a bearded jewelled Hoysala minister, a mason cutting rows of abstract pecking on a rock face, workers raising masonry round the colossus, bullock carts. Nits: the enclosure is drawn as a stepped block mass against the statue rather than a cloister wall round it; the line is cut on a cliff away from the statue.

scene-12: present-day Mahamastakabhisheka, priests in white pouring milk from a steel-and-timber scaffold, streams down the whole figure, a crowd with marigolds and saffron. Nit: today's enclosure walls and mantapa are absent.

No image shows a helmet, mail, a curved sword, a stirrup, a Mughal turban, a lion, boar or gandabherunda emblem, a Hoysala or Vijayanagara temple at close range, an enclosure wall before 1116, the stepped tank, modern letters on stone, or close frontal nudity; the colossus is shown feet-only, waist-up, or full-length at a distance with the crowd masking the lower half, and the monks are seated in side or back view; the general is the same man in all seven pictures that show him; no extra hands or fingers were found.
limitations: This is an AI review by a Claude agent; no human historian or epigraphist has read the text or checked the images.

Fact checking was limited to the research files in data/history-src/research (Rice 1889 archive.org djvu text, Narasimhachar 1923 page images, Hultzsch EI VII page text, Buchanan 1807 djvu text, Fleet EI VI transcription) and did not re-fetch the primary sources; the 1923 translations of nos. 121 and 122, the Bhujabali Charita's edition, the Rajavali Kathe's Kannada text, Asiatic Researches IX and Indian Antiquary II were not read at first hand by anyone on this project.

Pullabba's sallekhana, the name Gommata as the minister's pet name, the Tyagada relief's identification and its c. 983 date, the Bankapura coronation site, the 1004 end of the Gangas and the 981 computation rest on Nagarajaiah, Sarma, Krishna Rao, Kamath and popular datings as reported in the research, not on a primary text read here; the Chavundaraya Purana itself was not read.

No portrait of Chavundaraya survives; his face, the faces of every other person, the camp, the court, the writing room and the tenth-century buildings are invented, as the disclosure says. The colossus is a re-imagining from Rice's description and the Commons photographs, not a photograph.

Small far-distance details could not be verified individually: the shrines on Chandragiri and in the plain in the cover and scene-06 look slightly towered for the tenth century; scene-07 and scene-11 place the signature lines on the wrong part of the rock; scene-11's enclosure is drawn as a masonry mass; scene-12 lacks today's enclosure. These are recorded as nits and were not regenerated.

The images were judged at 1600x900 WebP with enlarged crops; the pseudo-strokes on scene-04's palm leaf and the pecked rows on scene-11's rock are not readable text and must not be taken as renderings of any inscription.
